source: original; stimulus is a public-domain photograph viewed before writing (see figures)

stimulus.source_note: Photograph: family watching television, about 1958. U.S. National Archives photograph by Evert F. Baumgardner, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.
stimulus.text: The photograph, taken about 1958, shows a family of five gathered around a small television set in their living room. Two children sit on the floor, a third lies in the foreground, and the parents watch with them, all facing the screen.

stem: The photograph best shows which change television brought to family life in the 1950s?

options.text: Families stopped eating meals together at home
options.misconception: The photograph shows a family together in one room, and it says nothing about meals.

options.text: Watching television became a shared evening activity at home
Parents banned their children from watching television
options.misconception: The photograph shows children watching with their parents, not banned from it.

options.text: Families sold their radios to pay for television sets
options.misconception: The photograph shows a television set, and it says nothing about radios or how the set was paid for.

rationales.A: The photograph shows a family together in one room, and it says nothing about meals.
rationales.B: The whole family sits facing one small screen together, so watching had become something the family did as a group.
rationales.C: The photograph shows children watching with their parents, not banned from it.
rationales.D: The photograph shows a television set, and it says nothing about radios or how the set was paid for.
rationales.general:
1. Look at what the people are doing: father, mother, and three children all face one small screen.
2. They sit together in the living room, not apart in separate rooms.
3. That picture is the new habit: an evening spent watching together at home.
Remember: When a photo shows a whole family doing one thing together, ask what shared habit it pictures.
